steps.a: Grandma told Aunt Jo that she had fallen in the pool.
steps.b: Grandma laughed. “Jo, you fell in the pool!”
steps.reveal: In the first sentence, “she” could be Grandma or Aunt Jo, so the reader has to guess. The second makes it clear. A pronoun only works when the reader knows exactly who it means.

cards.title: The antecedent
cards.body: The antecedent is the noun a pronoun stands for. In “Leo forgot his lunch,” the antecedent of “his” is Leo. Every pronoun needs an antecedent the reader can find.

cards.title: Agreement
cards.body: A pronoun must match its antecedent. One thing → it/its: “The tree lost its leaves.” More than one → they/their: “The trees lost their leaves.” A group acting as one → it/its: “The team won its match.” For one person whose gender you don’t know, “they/their” is fine: “Each student brought their lunch.”

cards.title: Unclear vs clear
cards.telling: Omar and Ben fixed his bike.
cards.showing: Omar and Ben fixed Omar’s bike.
cards.note: When two people could be “he”, “she” or “they”, use the name. Repeating a name is better than confusing the reader.

cards.title: Find the problem pronouns
cards.prompt: Tap the two pronouns that don’t agree with their antecedents.
cards.text: The puppies chased its ball across the yard. My sister found a wallet and returned them to the office.

prompts: Find one place in your paragraph where you chose a name instead of a pronoun. Why?
Why do clear pronouns matter even more in an essay than in a chat with a friend?
